# CI and CodeQL

<a id="ciとcodeql"></a>

`verify.yml` checks locked dependencies, asset inputs, every app, and generated-file synchronization. Changes to `codeql.yml` also trigger all app checks.

`codeql.yml` analyzes Actions, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java/Kotlin, and Swift on pushes to main, PRs targeting main, weekly runs, and manual runs. Actions and JS/TS run on Linux without a build. Kotlin compiles the Android app in debug mode on Linux. Swift prepares Pods on macOS and builds for Simulator without signing. These jobs do not change the SDK generation, distribution, DB, or production service settings.

Swift analysis uses `EXPO_USE_PRECOMPILED_MODULES=1`, matching the existing Podfile default. It uses frameworks supplied with the pinned npm dependencies to reduce the load of rebuilding external Expo dependencies from source and timing out before analysis. The custom `QrScanOcr` module has no precompiled setting and is built from source. Keep extraction checks for all five tracked Swift files, including the app and extensions, and also inspect actual extraction diagnostics. Missing extraction of managed source must not be treated as successful analysis.

The Swift analysis build specifies `ARCHS=arm64 ONLY_ACTIVE_ARCH=YES` to avoid duplicate arm64 and x86_64 builds for a generic Simulator destination timing out the job. Keep extraction checks for all tracked Swift files. This setting is confined to CI and does not change distribution build settings.

Swift Pods preparation runs `pod install` using the local Pod definitions from pinned npm dependencies and the source-build settings used for analysis. It does not reject local definitions missing from the existing Pods lock through deployment mode and thereby stop analysis. It uses the external Pod constraints in the existing lock and does not run `pod update`. Log runner-side lock changes; do not change the repository's native source, Podfile, or Pods lock. This prepares an analysis build; it does not complete distribution lock consistency checks or release acceptance.

Each job limits the built-in GitHub token permissions to reading source and registering Security results. Checkout does not persist credentials. No new secret, signing key, or EAS/Store credentials are required. Native jobs do not use compilation caches, to avoid mistaking cached compilation for analysis results.

The analysis step disables upload regardless of event type. After analysis, native jobs proceed only after verifying that every tracked Swift/Kotlin file is included in the source archive. Only non-PR runs satisfying the normal success conditions register results in the existing category through a later upload-sarif step. Failed analysis or inclusion checks prevent registration, so incomplete results do not replace existing analysis. PRs preserve Default setup and do not register results in Code scanning; after successful validation, they retain each language's SARIF as an artifact for seven days. Check every language job and artifact save, and verify native source-archive inclusion for all tracked Swift/Kotlin files. Archive inclusion is supporting evidence; inspect actual extraction diagnostics and analysis coverage separately. Unextracted source, build failures, or missing SARIF must not be treated as successful analysis.

Adoption has two stages. First, pin the Draft PR head and verify all four language jobs, SARIF artifacts, and actual source coverage while retaining Default setup. Native result registration in Code scanning has not been accepted at this stage. Then, when adoption of that head into main is approved, switch from Default to Advanced and read back uploads for each language after the main push and manual verification. Successful ongoing analysis and registration on main and weekly runs are post-adoption acceptance criteria; PR success alone is insufficient. Do not switch early and interrupt existing analysis or run both setups in parallel. This workflow does not change required rulesets. Native jobs, including macOS, increase runtime and Actions usage; inspect measured runs.

The first Swift build on main ran for about 58 minutes before the 60-minute job limit stopped it ahead of analysis. Swift therefore has a 90-minute window for build and analysis together. The other three languages retain 60-minute limits. Increasing the limit is not evidence of success: verify build, analysis, extraction of the five managed files, and result registration for the target SHA.
